newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Wave of mergers seen hitting Slovenian banks.
newsitem.headline: Wave of mergers seen hitting Slovenian banks.

text.p: A wave of mergers aimed at cutting costs and raising efficiency is expected to hit Slovenia's overcrowded banking industry before year's end, analysts said on Wednesday.
Slovenia, the smallest of the former Yugoslav republics with a population of just two million, currently boasts 29 registered banks, most of them small start-ups with tiny market share.

"There is not enough space in Slovenia for so many banks. In the next four years there will be just five or six bigger banks left," Aleksander Simon, an analyst at Nova ljubljanska banka, told Reuters.
A handful of banks have already announced merger plans to help cut their overheads and prepare for a harsher climate of competition once the sector is opened to foreign players.

"We need stronger banks because the smaller ones will find it very hard to compete with others when more foreign banks enter the Slovenian market," Peter Stanovnik, director of the Ljubljana Institute for Economic Research, said.

Parliament is expected to pass a new law next year, enabling foreign banks to establish branches in Slovenia in line with European Union regulations. Currently, foreign banks can only set up subsidiaries, requiring big capital outlays.

Foreshadowing the expected wave of consolidation in the industry, banks Gorenjska banka and UBK last week announced they were in talks about a possible merger, while Dolenjska bank also disclosed it had discussed a potential tie-up.

"By the end of the year we can expect at least two, if not three mergers. Smaller banks are much more vulnerable, so their wish to merge with stronger banks is just natural," said Toni Apollonio, an analyst at "A" bank.

Most of the country's banks hold retail market shares of less than five percent. The top three banks -- state owned Nova ljubljanska banka and Nova kreditna banka Maribor, and listed SKB -- control more than half of the market between them.

Analysts added that mergers were crucial to bring down the high interest rates that have hampered Slovenia's industrial recovery after the loss of key markets in other former Yugoslav republics when the country gained independence in 1991.

"The banks' problem is the high price of their services, which is reflected in a big spread between lending and deposit interest rates," said France Krizanic, an economic analyst at the Ljubljana Faculty of Law.
Average long-term commercial lending rates stood at 12.6 percent last month, while deposit rates were at 7.1 percent.

Market watchers said the consolidation trend among banks would also hit the country's 46 brokerage houses, which would see their business decline as the country's mass privatisation programme nears an end.
"By the end of the century the number of brokerages could fall to 10," said Apollonio.

Troubled financial consultancy Dadas and brokerage Primofin last week said they were planning a merger. Dadas, which has come under pressure after the stock market watchdog in March pushed to shut down its key Proficia Dadas fund, already owns around half of Primofin's shares.
